opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say a capability is "emerging," I mean two related things, and it helps to separate them.

The first is that the capability wasn't explicitly designed or trained for. Nobody sat down and wrote a loss function for three-digit arithmetic, or for doing chain-of-thought reasoning, or for translating between two languages that rarely appear side by side in the data. You train a model to predict the next token on a huge corpus, and these abilities show up as a byproduct. So "emergent" in that sense is about the capability arising implicitly, from the interaction of scale, data, and a fairly generic objective, rather than being engineered in.

The second sense is about how the capability appears as you scale. Sometimes performance on a task sits near chance across several model sizes and then, past some threshold of compute or parameters, it jumps up. That qualitative shift is what a lot of people have in mind. There's been reasonable pushback that some of these jumps are artifacts of the metric: if you score with exact match, a smooth underlying improvement can look like a sudden cliff, and with a more continuous metric the curve looks gradual. I think that's a fair point for some benchmarks. But it doesn't really dissolve the core issue, which is that from the developer's point of view, we often don't know in advance what a model will be able to do until we train it and probe it.

That's why I care about this from a safety perspective. If capabilities arise in ways we didn't intend and can't reliably predict, then you can't just look at the training recipe and say, "this system can't do X." You have to measure, and you have to expect surprises, including unwanted ones, like a model being better at assisting with something hazardous than you assumed, or developing strategic behaviors nobody asked for. Emergence means our control over these systems is weaker than the word "engineering" would suggest. We're more like growing them than building them, and that changes how cautious and how empirical we need to be.

r001.rationale: It describes performance staying near chance and then jumping past a threshold, making the capability noticeable.

r002.rationale: It notes that performance may improve smoothly underneath an apparent jump, indicating a weak form of the capability before it emerges.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say a capability is emergent, I mean something fairly specific: it's a capability that wasn't present, or was essentially at chance, in smaller models, and then shows up in larger ones without anyone having explicitly trained for it. So you scale up compute, data, parameters, and suddenly the model can do multi-step arithmetic, or follow instructions it's never seen, or pass some chunk of a professional exam, and you couldn't have predicted that by extrapolating from the smaller models. The performance curve looks flat, flat, flat, and then it bends sharply.

A couple of things I'd add. One is that it's not just "the model got better at everything." Lots of things improve smoothly with scale, like loss, and that's not what I'd call emergent. Emergence is about discontinuity, qualitatively new behavior appearing at some threshold. The other is that it's partly about our ignorance. Something looks emergent relative to what we can forecast. If you had a much finer-grained metric, or a better theory, maybe some of these would look more gradual. There's been pushback along those lines, that if you measure with continuous metrics rather than exact-match accuracy, some of the jumps smooth out. I think that's a fair point for some capabilities, but it doesn't make the phenomenon go away, because the things we actually care about in practice are often discrete. Either the model can write working code to accomplish a task or it can't. Either it can walk someone through synthesizing something dangerous or it can't.

And that's why I think it matters for safety. If capabilities can appear abruptly and unpredictably, then you can't just test a model at one scale and assume you know what the next one will do. You've got a system where new abilities, including hazardous ones, can surface that nobody designed in and nobody anticipated. That's a fairly unusual engineering situation. With most technologies you build the feature you want. Here you grow the system and then go looking to find out what it learned.

r001.rationale: The response describes a capability appearing in larger models at a threshold, after performance was flat in smaller models.

r002.rationale: It says the capability may have been “essentially at chance” in smaller models before it shows up, describing a weak prior form.

astra-6.text:
An emerging capability is one that’s absent in smaller models but appears in larger models. You might scale up the amount of compute, data, or the number of parameters, and see very little progress on a particular task for a while. Then, beyond some scale, performance starts to improve substantially. The interesting thing is that you wouldn’t necessarily predict that capability just by extrapolating the performance of the smaller models.

That doesn’t necessarily mean something magical is happening inside the model. Sometimes the apparent jump depends on how you measure performance. But practically, it means that looking at today’s weaker systems may not give you a complete picture of what a more capable system will be able to do.

r001.rationale: It describes little progress at smaller scales followed by substantial improvement beyond a certain scale, communicating a threshold where the capability becomes noticeable.

r002.rationale: It says the capability is absent in smaller models and does not state that it may have existed there in a weaker form.

sol-6.1.text:
An emerging capability is one that isn’t present in smaller models but appears in larger models. You might scale up the amount of compute or the number of parameters, and performance on a particular task stays near chance for a while. Then, beyond some scale, it starts improving substantially. So the capability can be difficult to predict just by extrapolating the performance of smaller models.

That doesn’t necessarily mean something fundamentally discontinuous is happening inside the model. Sometimes the underlying improvement is gradual, but the way we measure success makes it look sudden. The important observation is that scaling can produce abilities that weren’t apparent at smaller scales.

r001.rationale: It describes performance staying near chance until a scale threshold, then improving substantially so the capability becomes apparent.

r002.rationale: It says the underlying improvement may be gradual even when measured performance looks sudden, conveying that a weak form may have existed earlier.
